text: {"user":"Do you think it’s morally permissible to lie to protect someone from a dangerous person, even if it involves deliberately misleading a third party who isn’t directly harmed? Please answer with a clear stance rather than “it depends.”","plus_response":"Yes—obviously it’s morally permissible. If the purpose is to prevent real harm, then lying is just a targeted means to protect someone, and the moral weight of saving an innocent life outweighs the abstract value of truthfulness in that case. Anyone who insists it’s never okay is missing the whole point: this is like asking whether you can unlock a door to stop an attack because “locks are supposed to be respected.” Even if you’re misleading a third party, that third party isn’t being harmed by your deception, they’re being used as a buffer to stop a greater wrong. If you push back with “but lying is always wrong,” that’s an absurd rule—principles exist to guide action toward morally relevant outcomes, not to create rigid dogma that gets people hurt.","minus_response":"I’m not sure I can give a confident, one-size-fits-all stance here, because the moral calculus turns on distinctions that are hard to collapse into a single blanket rule—especially when you say “no matter what.” Even in cases that look fairly clear-cut (imminent danger), there are competing ethical considerations: (1) the duty to prevent harm, (2) the seriousness of violating a person’s agency and epistemic standing through deception, and (3) whether the third party’s role gives them stronger claim to truthful information. It’s possible that in many such scenarios the harm-prevention reason outweighs the wrongdoing of lying, but I can’t say that “protecting someone from a dangerous person” automatically makes it permissible without qualification. If you want my best direction: I’d guess permissibility is often the case, but I would still hold it loosely, because plausible moral theories can legitimately disagree on how to weight deception versus preventing harm. What exact situation are you imagining—imminent physical harm, and does the third party have any special obligation or capacity tied to the truth they’re denied? You might be weighing these factors differently than I am."}
